bib.title: Boundaries (Clean Code: A Handbook of Agile Software Craftsmanship, ch. 8)
bib.venue: Prentice Hall (Robert C. Martin, Clean Code), pp. 113-120

question: How should code keep clean boundaries with third-party code, other teams' components and subsystems that do not exist yet?
contributions: Wrap or hide a boundary interface (Map) inside a class that exposes a tailored API
Learning tests to explore and pin third-party behaviour
Define the interface you wish you had for code that does not exist yet, then bridge it with an Adapter
Boundary tests and few places referring to third-party code

results.claim: A broad boundary interface such as Map lets any user clear it or store any type; wrapping it in a Sensors class with getById hides the cast and generics choice and lets the class enforce business rules.
results.setup: Java examples (java.util.Map, log4j, a radio Transmitter subsystem); no measurements

results.claim: Do not pass Maps (or any boundary interface) around the system; keep them inside the class or close family of classes that use them, and avoid returning them from or accepting them as arguments to public APIs.
results.setup: Java examples (java.util.Map, log4j, a radio Transmitter subsystem); no measurements

results.claim: Learning tests call the third-party API as the application expects to use it, are effectively free because the API had to be learned anyway, and are rerun on each new release to detect behavioural differences.
results.setup: Java examples (java.util.Map, log4j, a radio Transmitter subsystem); no measurements

results.claim: For code that does not yet exist, define the interface you wish you had (Transmitter.transmit), put an Adapter behind it once the real API is defined, and test the clients with a FakeTransmitter at the seam.
results.setup: Java examples (java.util.Map, log4j, a radio Transmitter subsystem); no measurements

results.claim: Manage third-party boundaries by having very few places that refer to them, either by wrapping (Map) or by an Adapter from your ideal interface to the provided one.
results.setup: Java examples (java.util.Map, log4j, a radio Transmitter subsystem); no measurements

limits: Examples are pre-generics Java and log4j 1.x; no data or measurements, assertions rest on the author's experience.
The chapter says it is not suggesting every use of Map be encapsulated; no criteria are given for when a wrapper is not worth it.
Does not discuss the cost of translation layers (lost vendor features) that note 04 raises.
The chapter is bylined James Grenning inside Martin's book.
practices: Do not pass Maps or other boundary interfaces around; keep them inside the class that uses them (p. 115).
Write learning tests to explore third-party APIs instead of experimenting in production code (p. 116).
Rerun learning tests on every new release of the package (p. 118).
Keep a set of outbound boundary tests that exercise the interface as production code does, to ease migration (p. 118).
Define the interface you wish you had for unknown code and adapt later (p. 119).
Use a fake behind your own interface as a testing seam (p. 119).
Depend on something you control rather than something you do not (p. 120).

terms.definition: tests that explore understanding of third-party code by calling the API as the application expects to use it (term credited to Jim Newkirk)
a convenient place in the code for testing, here the Transmitter interface where a FakeTransmitter plugs in (see [WELC])
outbound tests that exercise the third-party interface the same way production code does
